title: Flu Season Hits Washington Early as Health Officials Report First Deaths
excerpt: Snohomish County confirms its first flu death of the fall while hospitalizations reach December-level rates weeks ahead of schedule.
body:
• Snohomish County confirmed its first influenza death of the season on Oct. 3 — an Edmonds man in his 70s with underlying conditions who tested positive for influenza A — as flu hospitalizations in the county reached levels usually not seen until December.
  • A Thurston County death initially reported Oct. 7 as the season's first was later reclassified: health officials said symptoms began in September, technically placing it in the prior season's count.
  • Seattle Children's recorded about 150 pediatric flu cases in two weeks, up from roughly 10 in the same stretch last fall — a level its infectious disease chief calls "about two months early."
  • A flu shot takes about two weeks to build full protection, so vaccinating now covers late-October Diwali and November Thanksgiving gatherings; first-time vaccine recipients ages 6 months through 8 years need two doses at least four weeks apart.

Snohomish County has recorded its first influenza-related death of the fall as flu activity climbs weeks ahead of schedule across western Washington, prompting health officials to warn that the 2026-27 season may peak earlier and more intensely than in recent years.

The death, on Oct. 3, was that of an Edmonds man in his 70s who had underlying health conditions and tested positive for influenza A, the county health department said. It marks the earliest first death in the county in at least three years; in prior seasons it arrived in November.

"We are at levels typically seen in early December, which may be a sign of an earlier-than-normal peak season."

— Hollianne Bruce, lead epidemiologist, Snohomish County Health Department

An early and accelerated arrival

Flu accounted for 1.7% of emergency department visits in Snohomish County — above the 1.4% state threshold for elevated community transmission. Since Aug. 30, 63 county residents have been hospitalized with influenza, including 31 in a single week, health officials said.

https://x.com/WFLA/status/2108924526218428796

The pattern is repeating across the West. About 150 children tested positive for influenza across the Seattle Children's hospital system over a recent two-week stretch, compared with about 10 in the same period last fall, according to an Oct. 4 report in The Washington Post cited by Becker's Hospital Review.

"We're about two months early. The way flu is circulating now, you wanted that vaccine in you two weeks ago, if not even a little before that."

— Dr. Danielle Zerr, head of pediatric infectious diseases, Seattle Children's

Early surveillance in Washington shows influenza A (H1N1) predominating, a shift from last season when H3N2 dominated. The University of Washington's Helen Chu told The Post that people may have less recent immunity against this year's leading strain. Nationally, 3.4% of clinical lab specimens tested positive during the week ending Sept. 26, and the CDC estimates infections are growing in 48 states.

Why it matters now

Context tempers the alarm: 2024-25 was Washington's worst flu season in eight years — more than 380 deaths statewide, with 53 deaths and 859 hospitalizations in Snohomish County alone — while 2025-26 was comparatively lighter at 24 county deaths. The early start this year has officials warning against complacency.

One wrinkle: Thurston County Public Health initially announced its first 2026-27 flu death on Oct. 7, then corrected the release a day later — symptoms began in September, so the death counts toward the 2025-26 season. As of Oct. 7, the county's respiratory virus activity was "below transmission alert," and statewide influenza-like illness remained minimal: 1.1% of outpatient visits against a 2.1% baseline.

What you can do

County Health Officer Dr. James Lewis urged residents to get vaccinated, and county officials advise getting a flu shot one to two weeks before social gatherings to allow immunity time to build. The CDC's guidance is unchanged: an annual flu vaccine for everyone 6 months and older, with people 65 and older benefiting from higher-dose formulations.

A flu shot takes about two weeks to build full protection, and children ages 6 months through 8 years who are receiving a flu vaccine for the first time — or have had only one dose before — need two doses at least four weeks apart. Starting that series now may not yield full protection until November, which is why officials are pressing parents not to wait.

Basic precautions remain the cheapest defense: wash hands with soap for at least 20 seconds, avoid touching the face, stay home when sick, and isolate sick household members, Thurston County health officials advised. People at elevated risk — adults 65 and older, children under 5, pregnant people, and those who are immunocompromised or have chronic conditions — should contact a clinician promptly if symptoms appear, since early antiviral treatment can blunt severity. Flu shots are available at most pharmacies, clinics, and provider offices.
